person.name: Vansh Pandit
person.schema_description: BS-MS student in applied mathematics at IISER Thiruvananthapuram working in computer vision, with most of his work so far in medical image analysis.

paragraphs_html: I am a fourth-year BS-MS student in applied mathematics at IISER Thiruvananthapuram, and computer vision is the thing I keep coming back to. Most of my work so far has been on medical images — finding what matters in a scan, turning it into numbers that hold up, predicting something a clinician actually needs to know — but the questions that keep me there are not really about medicine.

What I care about is generalisation. A model that scores well on the data it was trained on can fall apart on data it has never seen, and I would rather have a small model whose reasoning I can follow than a large one I have to take on trust. That problem turns up everywhere — different hospitals and scanners, streets in weather nobody photographed, terrain a simulator invented — which is how I have ended up chasing it through PET/CT, ultrasound, driving scenes and a drone.
intro.now_html: building the B-mode radiomics pipeline for QuantUS at TU Dresden, and looking for a master's thesis for next year. Medical imaging is the likeliest home for it, but I would happily be talked into another corner of vision.

updates.html: First paper out. Geometry Meets Metabolism placed in the top 15 at the MICCAI 2026 HECKTOR challenge.
Wrapped up the PET/CT oncology work at IIT Jammu; code and feature tables released publicly.
Started on the QuantUS B-mode radiomics pipeline with TU Dresden.

interests.heading: Research interests
interests.lead_html: I want vision systems that earn trust: robust before they are clever, interpretable before they are state of the art. Whether a model points at the right thing matters to me more than where it lands on a leaderboard. Medicine is where that bar is hardest to clear, which is why most of my work lives there — but the same question follows me anywhere a model has to cope with data nobody showed it.

publication.heading: Publication
publication.title: Geometry Meets Metabolism: Interpretable Segmentation, Staging, and Prognosis in Head and Neck PET/CT
publication.authors_html: V. Pandit et al. · team Vision-II · August 2026
publication.badge: Ranked in the top 15 of the challenge
paragraphs_html: The challenge pools head-and-neck PET/CT scans from several hospitals and asks three clinical questions at once: outline the primary tumour and the involved lymph nodes, assign the tumour and nodal stage, and predict recurrence-free survival. We built one pipeline for all three, and designed every component for stability across centres rather than for the leaderboard.

That constraint decided the design. Nodal stage is read directly off a few geometric measurements of the segmented nodes, chiefly a greatest-dimension diameter that mirrors the size criterion a radiologist already uses, then refined by a fixed rule on metabolic activity. Tumour stage fuses a tabular classifier with a convolutional network on a tumour-centred crop. Survival is a Cox model over clinical variables and predicted stage, with imaging deliberately left out because it is the most scanner-dependent part of the pipeline. Every staging and survival component was selected by its accuracy on a hospital held out during development, not by its average.

Two results I did not expect: for nodal staging the plain geometric head beat every image model we tried, on the average centre and on the weakest one; and for survival, nothing with more capacity beat a linear model.

figures.caption_html: The pipeline. Segmentation feeds both staging heads; the survival model deliberately does not use the masks. The flame marks a learned component, the blue tag marks a fixed rule with no training at all.
figures.alt: Three-stage pipeline diagram. Stage one crops a co-registered PET/CT pair to 3.27 mm and segments the primary tumour and nodes with a five-fold nnU-Net, scored by Dice. Stage two derives nodal stage from six geometric features of the segmented nodes, including greatest diameter, count and laterality, through an ordinal gradient booster and a fixed PET activity gate at tau 2.5; tumour stage fuses an ImageNet-initialised ConvNeXt on a 140 mm crop with a gradient-boosted tabular model over seventeen shape and PET features, weighted 60 image to 40 tabular. Stage three predicts recurrence-free survival with a Cox proportional-hazards model over clinical variables and predicted stage only, with imaging deliberately excluded as scanner-dependent.
figures.zoom_label: Open the pipeline diagram at full size

figures.caption_html: Why these components. Blue is the mean over held-out centres, orange is the worst one. Selecting on the worst centre instead of the mean is what put the geometric head and the linear survival model into the final pipeline.
figures.alt: Three bar charts comparing candidate models for nodal staging, tumour staging and survival. Each candidate shows a blue bar for the mean over held-out centres and an orange bar for the worst held-out centre. The geometric nodal head, the ConvNeXt tumour model and the Cox survival model are outlined as the chosen components.

items.title: Reading ultrasound before it becomes a picture
paragraphs_html: I develop the core B-mode radiomics pipeline of QuantUS, an open-source quantitative ultrasound platform. It computes first-order and GLCM texture features directly from raw RF signals, before the beamformed grey image most people picture as an ultrasound exists.

The features are the easy half. The hard half is making a number mean the same thing on two different machines, so I implemented phantom-based normalisation for device-independent, reproducible results. I also work on backend refactoring and GUI integration, because a method is only useful if a clinical researcher can reach it.

items.title: Segmenting things no dataset warned you about
paragraphs_html: A vision system that only recognises what it was shown is a liability on a real road. I built a pipeline for semantic segmentation of both known and novel objects, extending AIDE with lightweight captioning models (GLAMM, CODA-LM) so the system can describe what it cannot yet classify. Prototyped on Cityscapes, benchmarked on IDD, IDD-Anomaly and Carla-Anomaly.
This is the project that decided the rest. Segmentation was the first time I could watch the mathematics do something visible.

items.title: Rebuilding machine learning before trusting it
paragraphs_html: A summer implementing classical and Bayesian machine-learning models from scratch in NumPy, then comparing them honestly against their scikit-learn equivalents on real data. The library call is one line; knowing why it converges is the education.

items.title: Teaching a drone to stay out of sight
paragraphs_html: A custom 3D Gymnasium environment with simplified flight physics, 12-ray LiDAR sensing, procedurally generated terrain and moving observers with limited fields of view. I shaped a multi-objective reward and trained a PPO agent with Stable-Baselines3 and curriculum learning until it could reach its waypoints while staying out of the observers' cones.
I also built interactive visualisers in Pygame and Ursina, because watching a policy fly is a much faster way to learn what it has understood than reading a reward curve.

items.text_html: I grew up in Kashmir and moved most of the length of India to study by the Arabian Sea. The plan was biology, but my Class XII stream did not offer it, so I took applied mathematics and spent the early years deliberately sampling fields until one stuck. Medical imaging turned out to be the way back to the first plan.
Schooled in Jammu, made in Kashmir.
